analysis.summary: Engineering has the larger dollar overrun: $12m above annual plan, versus $5m for Sales & marketing. It also has a reported capability gap, making spend effectiveness the first investigation priority. These are annual run-rate comparisons at September 30, 2026—not quarterly actual overspend.

sections.text: At September 30, 2026, Engineering’s annual loaded workforce cost is $420m, with a positive $12m variance above comparable annual plan. Sales & marketing is $180m, with a positive $5m variance above plan. Costs include overtime and contractors. Engineering is the first priority on absolute dollars; this does not establish which function has the larger percentage overrun.

sections.title: The operational context differs
sections.text: Engineering has a reported capability gap of 16 FTE, versus 0 for Sales & marketing, as of September 30. Meanwhile, Sales & marketing has higher annualized voluntary attrition: 10.0%, versus Engineering’s 7.0%, based on July–September 2026. sections.title: First: reconcile Engineering’s overrun to the capability it buys
sections.text: Ask Finance and Engineering for a plan-to-run-rate reconciliation separating staffing volume, pay rates and job mix, contractors, overtime, and hiring timing. Map incremental spending to the capabilities and delivery commitments it supports. The key question is whether above-plan spending is closing the assessed gap, providing temporary cover, or funding work that can be stopped. Avoid a blanket hiring freeze until that distinction is clear.

sections.title: Second: examine Sales & marketing’s replacement and compensation costs
sections.text: Run the same cost reconciliation for Sales & marketing, with particular attention to replacement hiring, temporary overlap, and variable compensation against plan and commercial results. Higher attrition makes replacement-related costs worth testing, but it does not establish their contribution. Separate justified performance-linked pay from controllable overspend.

turns.answerTitle: Engineering’s readiness gap strengthens the concern—not evidence of broad hiring or retention failure

analysis.summary: Investigate Engineering first for spend effectiveness: its larger dollar variance coexists with a capability shortfall and weaker succession coverage than Sales & marketing. However, aggregate hiring speed and voluntary attrition do not indicate worse performance in Engineering. The evidence supports investigation, not a conclusion that spending is wasteful.

sections.title: The strongest supporting signals are capability and succession readiness
sections.text: At September 30, 2026, Engineering’s annual workforce cost run rate is $12m above plan, versus $5m for Sales & marketing. Engineering also reports a 16 FTE capability gap, versus 0 for Sales, and ready-now succession coverage of 66.7%, versus 75.0%. These strengthen the concern that higher spending is not yet accompanied by sufficient readiness; they do not establish that the cost variance caused the gaps.

sections.title: Two counter-signals limit the diagnosis
sections.text: For July–September 2026, Engineering’s time to fill is 44.9 days versus Sales & marketing’s 46.6 days. Its annualized voluntary attrition is also lower: 7.0% versus 10.0%. Thus, the aggregate evidence does not support slower hiring or higher turnover as Engineering’s distinguishing problem. Time to fill covers filled roles, while the attrition figures are annualized observations—not forecasts.

sections.title: A skill-mix or timing mismatch is plausible
sections.text: Engineering may be spending on capacity that is still ramping, on skills outside the measured shortage, or on temporary coverage while scarce capabilities develop. Alternatively, the higher spending may be justified investment against future delivery needs. Skill-specific readiness dates, spending components and delivery outcomes would distinguish these explanations.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.text: The comparison establishes a larger dollar variance, not a larger percentage overrun or lower productivity. Engineering’s annual loaded workforce cost is $420m, versus $180m for Sales & marketing, so scale matters. These are September-end annual run rates, not quarterly actual overspend. The retrieved evidence does not explain the variance by payroll, contractors, overtime or hiring mix, connect it to delivery results, or establish whether capability assessments cover comparable needs across functions. All figures are synthetic.

sections.title: Start with a cost-to-readiness review, not a blanket cost cut
sections.text: Ask Finance and Engineering to reconcile the variance by cost driver, then map the capability shortfall to funded work, required skills, assessed readiness and delivery deadlines. Check whether spending is closing those specific gaps and whether uncovered priority roles overlap critical delivery dependencies. Use that review to distinguish justified ramp-up investment from persistent allocation problems.

unknowns: Which cost components and approved business changes explain the variance?
Are the capability gaps temporary ramp-up gaps or persistent shortages in critical skills?
What delivery outcomes and business value accompany the additional spending?
followups: Check whether cost variance and capability readiness have improved or deteriorated over time.
